---
title: "Preface"
---

Most spatial books teach a library. This one teaches the data.

There are only a handful of ideas in spatial computing, and they wear different
costumes in every tool, format and domain. Three threads run through every chapter
of this book.

**Projection is the universal verb.** Geographic to projected coordinates is a
projection. Projected coordinates to grid index space is rasterization. Index
space back to coordinates is extraction. The affine transform is the bridge
between them. These are one operation applied at different stages of the pipeline.

**Representation is the problem.** Antimeridian wrapping, polygon splitting,
topology that is built and then discarded, cos(latitude) weights on a global mean:
these are artefacts of the coordinate system or the data structure, not of the
geometry. Change the representation and the problem goes away. Warp the grid.
Normalise the vertices. Address pixels by index.

**Decomposition reveals choices.** A coordinate reference system is a family, a
centre and some parameters. A grid is six numbers. A geometry is one of five
table forms. The standard tooling hands you an opaque bundle; the insight comes
from pulling it apart into independent decisions you can make for your own data
and your own question.

The examples come from real datasets: OISST and GHRSST sea surface temperature,
NSIDC sea ice, AVISO currents, CCAMLR management areas, GEBCO bathymetry, Southern
Ocean model output. They are the datasets where the author learned these lessons,
usually the hard way.

This is a working draft. Chapters include harvested fragments more or less as they
were written; the seams show.
